source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina, Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning?
finding: 3 of 6 wild-caught crows learned a two-trap tube with a tool, then passed two transfers that removed arbitrary cues. All 3 failed transfer 3 (one functional trap with a base, one hole with no base). All 3 then passed a visually different trap-table. The paper first read this as causal and analogical reasoning; the two-hole failure shows the rule was keyed to the hole, not the base.
numbers: Initial tube: criterion 17/20 over two blocks (alpha 0.01); learners needed 103.3 +/- 20.3 trials (150-trial cap). Transfers 1 and 2 passed (15/20 criterion). Transfer 3 failed; highest latency and side-switching of any transfer (p = 0.0156). Trap-table: all 3 correct on first trial; the 3 non-learners failed it. 10 of 12 first transfer trials avoided the trap, but first-trial success did not predict later success (Tiga and Slevin correct on trial 1 of transfer 3, then chance for 19 trials).
quote: the crows had knowledge of the meat's relation with the hole as a proximate causal regularity but did not infer the existence of a distal causal mechanism
limits: N = 6 birds, 3 learners. Only learners switched probing side (22.1% vs 0%, U=9, p=0.032), so inhibitory control may decide who learns.
agent_relevance: Passing a far transfer (table) while failing a near one (two holes) means a pass shows a rule keyed to one feature, not the deeper cause. Do not credit the agent with a mechanism from one transfer pass. Test the near variant that breaks the shallow rule.

source: Taylor (2020) Folk Physics for Crows?
finding: The first author of the 2009 study now reads the two-hole failure and the weight-inattention result as support for Povinelli's claim: crows track observable regularities, not unobservable forces such as gravity. He also warns it is too early to say they cannot, because task format changes results a lot.
numbers: Cites: apes do better when they can pull than push (Mulcahy & Call 2006); crows infer weight from wind (Jelbert 2019); crows preplan metatool solutions (Gruber 2019); crows react to a hidden agent (Taylor et al 2012).
quote: Clearly, at present, there does not seem to be any evidence that NC crows reason about unobservable causal mechanisms.
limits: Single-author review of one lab's programme. Proposes a ladder of probes in one paradigm: hidden object, then hidden agent, then unobservable mechanism, so failures are not due to jumps in task complexity.
agent_relevance: Mirror rule for the agent: a failure on one probe is weak evidence of absence. Run a ladder of increasing-difficulty probes in the same format before concluding a limit.

source: Neilands, Jelbert, Breen, Schiestl, Taylor (2016) How insightful is 'insight'? NC crows do not attend to object weight
finding: A signature test: seemingly insightful stone dropping onto a platform ignored object weight, which the contact account predicts and the force account does not. The same birds later preferred heavy blocks once trained.
numbers: 12 crows; only 2 spontaneously dropped blocks. D4R dropped heavy 12 times and light 22 times (p=0.062). The other 10 crows, after shaping to stone-drop, chose the heavy block on 125/140 trials (p<0.001), 3 birds 10/10. Pre-test: light block pulled out in 128/240 trials (p=0.167).
quote: New Caledonian crows exhibit a weight inattention error: they do not attend to the weight of an object when innovating stone dropping.
limits: Only 2 of 12 innovated, so the key result rests on 2 birds. Later preference for heavy shows the crows could detect weight; the error was one of experience, not capacity.
agent_relevance: Method for the agent: find the error signature that separates two accounts of a success. A right answer reached by a shallow rule shows itself in the specific mistakes it makes.

source: Jelbert, Taylor, Gray, et al. (2019) NC crows infer the weight of objects from observing their movements in a breeze
finding: Counterpoint to the weight-inattention result: in a different paradigm, crows used wind-driven motion to infer which novel object was light or heavy before handling it.
numbers: 35/48 first touches correct in the fan-on condition (72.9%, Wilcoxon p=0.01); 23/48 (47.9%) fan-off control. First test per bird: 11/12 correct fan-on (p=0.003), 6/12 control. First drop correct 44/48 (92%) fan-on, 38/48 (79%) fan-off.
limits: 12 birds; correct drop was high even in control (79%), so the touch measure carries the effect. Inference came from observed motion, not shown to be force reasoning.
agent_relevance: The same animal passes or fails on the same concept depending on task format. A limit found in one probe is a limit of that probe plus that animal's route to the answer.

source: Tebbich, Seed, Emery, Clayton (2007) Non-tool-using rooks solve the trap-tube problem
finding: Rooks without tool use can learn to avoid the trap, but none passed the novel transfers, so no evidence of causal understanding.
numbers: 3 of 7 rooks solved the modified trap-tube. 0 of those passed the new transfer tasks.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Learning to solve is not understanding. The transfer test separates them, and most animals fail it.

source: Seed, Call, Emery, Clayton (2009) Chimpanzees solve the trap problem when the confound of tool-use is removed
finding: Removing the tool from the trap-tube let all chimpanzees learn it. Task format, not only cognition, set earlier failures.
numbers: 8/8 chimps learned in 40 to 100 trials; 1 of 8 transferred to two tasks with no shared visual cue. 15 chimps in a 2x2 (experience x tool): significant effects of tool inclusion and experience, p<.05.
limits: Abstract only read. Transfer shown by one chimp only.
agent_relevance: Before judging a limit, remove task constraints that are not about the concept. For the agent: check that the probe format (output length, tool use, prompt) is not the barrier.

source: Girndt, Meier, Call (2008) Task constraints mask great apes' ability to solve the trap-table task
finding: Apes failed the usual two-rake trap-table above chance (replicating earlier work), but when they could choose where to insert a single tool most succeeded on trial 1.
numbers: 20 chimpanzees, 7 orangutans, 5 bonobos, 5 gorillas. With a single tool, about 80% solved on the first trial.
limits: Abstract only read. Taylor 2009 notes a prior disposition to avoid holes was not excluded.
agent_relevance: A pass can reflect a built-in avoidance rather than a learned one; use a control group that never trained.

source: Martin-Ordas, Call, Colmenares (2008) Tubes, tables and traps: apes solve two equivalent trap tasks but no transfer
finding: Four ape species solved a trap-tube and a functionally matched trap-platform task, yet showed no transfer across them and no correlation in performance between them.
numbers: Larger sample than prior studies, all four great ape species; apes did better on trap-platform than trap-tube; no correlation across tasks; no interspecies differences.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Competence on one task does not imply carry-over to a same-structure task. Expect to measure transfer, not assume it.

source: Horner & Whiten (2007) Learning from others' mistakes? Limits on understanding a trap-tube task by young chimpanzees and children
finding: Observing a model's errors did not speed learning in chimpanzees (ages 2 to 7) or 3 to 4 year-old children. Two of 6 chimps made anticipatory strategies with no evidence of representing the causal relation.
numbers: 6 chimpanzees; children aged 3 to 4 and 5 to 6. The 5 to 6 year-olds mastered the task without benefit from observing errors.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Young children also fail the trap-tube, so failure alone is not evidence of a non-human limit. Human baselines matter.

source: Penn, Holyoak, Povinelli (2008) Darwin's mistake: explaining the discontinuity between human and nonhuman minds
finding: The strong theory behind the limits: the gap is higher-order relational reasoning, approximating a physical symbol system. A hypothesis, not a finding.
numbers: No new data; target article with commentary in BBS.
limits: Abstract only read. Contested by many commentaries; Taylor 2009 presented crow transfer as against it.
agent_relevance: The rival theory against which a transfer pass is read. For the agent, relational transfer is the open question.

source: Hennefield, Hwang, Weston, Povinelli (2018) Meta-analytic techniques reveal corvid causal reasoning in Aesop's Fable paradigm is trial-and-error
finding: Pooled over 5 articles and 32+ experiments, corvids learned only from successful actions, not unsuccessful ones, and did not transfer across task variants. The authors conclude the paradigm cannot tell trial-and-error from causal reasoning.
numbers: Five articles, over 32 experiments (rooks, crows, jays). Follows Ghirlanda & Lind 2017: initial preference for functional objects plus trial-and-error may account for key variants.
limits: Abstract only read. Authors are from the Povinelli lab, which argues the limits view.
agent_relevance: Many apparent reasoning passes dissolve when trial-level learning is modelled. For the agent, log per-attempt learning curves, not only final success.

source: Zhang, Yu, Chen, Li (2021) Performance of Azure-winged magpies in Aesop's fable paradigm
finding: A new corvid species showed the usual profile: preferred functional cues (water over sand, heavy over light, solid over hollow) but failed tube diameter, water level and the counterintuitive U-tube, so partly trial-and-error.
numbers: Passed: water/sand, heavy/light, solid/hollow cue tasks. Failed: diameter, water level, U-tube.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Same pattern again: selective success on cues, failure on tasks that break the shortcut.

source: Gruber, Schiestl, Boeckle, et al. (2019) NC crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems
finding: Counter to earlier failed string-simulation tests: crows kept in mind out-of-sight tools and apparatuses and planned a multi-step sequence.
numbers: Abstract claims first conclusive evidence that birds plan several moves ahead while using tools.
limits: Abstract only read. Same species that failed to simulate string earlier (Taylor et al 2010, 2012, per Taylor 2020).
agent_relevance: Limits found with one material (string) were not general limits. Re-test with different materials and structure before writing a limit into the schema.

source: Taylor, Miller, Gray (2012) NC crows reason about hidden causal agents
finding: Crows inspected the hide and abandoned probing more often after an unexplained stick movement than after movement preceded by a human visibly entering. Authors read this as inference to a hidden cause.
numbers: 8 crows; two series of events (human enters hide, stick moves, human leaves, versus stick moves with no human).
limits: Abstract only read. Boogert et al 2013 and Dymond et al 2013 argued the controls were unbalanced and an associative account could fit.
agent_relevance: A contested positive. Same group, same species: hidden-agent inference claimed positive, gravity inference negative.

source: Boogert, Arbilly, Muth, Seed (2013) Do crows reason about causes or agents? The devil is in the controls
finding: A critique of Taylor 2012: the control conditions were not balanced, so an associative account could explain the crows' behaviour.
numbers: No new data in the item I saw.
limits: Letter; text not read. Taylor 2020 says associative accounts do not explain the full result.
agent_relevance: The failed-control pattern: a pass is only as good as its controls. Same lesson for agent evaluations.

source: Wu, Qiu, Ross, Akyurek, et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: Across 11 tasks (arithmetic in other bases, code with 1-based indexing, chess variants, altered chord tunings, and others), GPT-4 and other models did well on default versions and fell substantially on counterfactual versions with the same reasoning procedure. This is the language-model analogue of the two-hole tube.
numbers: 11 tasks; GPT-4 0-shot CoT 'consistently and substantially underperforms' on counterfactuals, though above chance. The gap shrinks but stays substantial with up to 16-shot CoT for bases 9, 11 and 16, and the gain plateaus. Counterfactual comprehension checks show models understand the new rules.
quote: If models implement a general and transferable task-solving procedure, we expect comparable performance on counterfactual and default tasks
limits: Task-specific. Default performance partly reflects memorisation (base-10 accuracy falls more slowly with digits). Authors say skills are not absent but narrow.
agent_relevance: Run a counterfactual twin of each test the agent must pass. A pass on the default form is a pass on the trap-tube, not on gravity.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogy problems from Webb et al 2023 re-run with permuted or symbol alphabets. Humans stayed high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 dropped sharply as the alphabet changed.
numbers: Overall accuracy (my reading of Table 2): humans 0.753 (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Counterfactual comprehension checks were mostly high, so models understood the new alphabets.
limits: Letter-string domain only; 2023 models. Table labels were read from a text extract.
agent_relevance: The best-controlled match to the crows: a pass on the familiar form (standard alphabet) does not carry to same-structure variants (altered alphabet).

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: A short replication and critique of Webb et al 2023: training-data overlap cannot be excluded and human tests may not measure models validly; simple variations break GPT-3 while humans stay high.
numbers: On synthetic-alphabet versions of extend sequence, successor, predecessor and fix-alphabetic-sequence, GPT-3 generative accuracy was below 0.1. Only remove-redundant and sort reached the original range. Counterfactual comprehension checks reached at least 30% of the original level in all but one case.
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) only. Human data from the authors' small online study.
agent_relevance: Same failure curve: a benchmark pass is not evidence of zero-shot generality unless contamination and surface cues are controlled.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: The claim being tested: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on non-visual matrix reasoning and other analogy tasks, zero-shot; early GPT-4 tests were better.
numbers: Abstract: GPT-3 'matching or even surpassing human capabilities in most settings'.
limits: Abstract only read. Challenged by Hodel & West and by Lewis & Mitchell with counterfactual variants.
agent_relevance: The positive pole of the same debate; the answer comes from the transfer variants, not the original.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: On ConceptARC (core-knowledge concept tasks), humans were far ahead of text GPT-4 and image GPT-4V. Better one-shot prompting helped a little, not to human level.
numbers: ConceptARC 480 tasks: humans 91%, first-place Kaggle program 52%, GPT-4 25% with simple zero-shot (Moskvichev et al). Detailed one-shot prompt: GPT-4 0.33 at both temperatures (versus 0.19 and 0.25 before). 48 minimal tasks: humans 0.95, GPT-4 0.69 and 0.65, GPT-4V 0.25 zero-shot and 0.23 one-shot.
limits: 2023 models. GPT-4V failures may include vision, not only reasoning. Prompt change moved accuracy by 8 to 14 points, so prompt format matters.
agent_relevance: On concept-level abstraction, run the minimal form first; failure even there is informative.

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks
finding: A claimed theory-of-mind success (GPT-3.5 on the unexpected-contents task) reversed under small changes that keep the same principles. The paper argues the zero-hypothesis should be that a pass is a shortcut until alterations are passed.
numbers: On the original prompts (Kosinski) the model gave P(popcorn)=100% for content and P(chocolate)=99% for the first belief prompt; under alterations the outputs changed to inconsistent values (exact conditions in paper; not recorded here).
limits: Informal small prompt study; one model family; others argue later models do better.
agent_relevance: Same shape as the crow case: alterations that keep the principle expose the rule actually used.

source: Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Shahrokhi, Tuzel, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) GSM-Symbolic: limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Changing only the numbers in grade-school maths questions lowers accuracy and raises variance; adding one irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp) cuts accuracy sharply for all models. Authors say models replicate steps rather than reason.
numbers: Up to 65% performance drop across state-of-the-art models from one added clause; accuracy also falls and variance rises as the number of clauses grows.
limits: Industry preprint, ICLR 2025; newer models may differ; some of the drop may be distractor handling, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Add NoOp-style distractors to the agent's test set. Salient irrelevant features pull the agent as the hole pulled the crows.

source: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar (2025) The illusion of thinking
finding: On controllable puzzles, reasoning models show a complete accuracy collapse beyond a complexity threshold and use fewer thinking tokens as problems get harder; standard models beat reasoning models on easy puzzles.
numbers: Three regimes: low complexity, standard models win; medium, reasoning models win; high, both collapse. Models fail to use explicit algorithms.
limits: Contested (next item). The meaning of 'collapse' is disputed.
agent_relevance: A limit curve for the agent: measure accuracy against depth and set a budget cut-off rather than adding more thinking at the collapse point.

source: Lawsen (2025) The illusion of the illusion of thinking
finding: A rebuttal: the 'collapse' reflects output token limits, unsolvable River Crossing instances (N >= 6 with the given boat capacity), and scoring that cannot tell cannot-solve from will-not-enumerate.
numbers: Hanoi failures at large N tied to output limits; models state they will stop to avoid length. Asking for a generating function instead of every move gave high accuracy in preliminary tests.
limits: Short comment with preliminary experiments; written with an AI co-author as disclosed in the paper. Not a full re-run.
agent_relevance: The 'limits found' can come from the probe: check output budget, solvability and scoring before writing a limit into the schema.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock, Dobbie (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: A benchmark for abstract reasoning beyond memorisation finds very limited LLM performance versus other NLP tasks, even with prompting techniques that help elsewhere.
numbers: Abstract only read; exact figures not recorded.
limits: Abstract only read. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Another source of the narrow-success pattern.

source: Ivanova (2024) Toward best research practices in AI psychology
finding: Fourteen methodology items for cognitive tests of LLMs: check what the model saw in training, test alternative strategies, add control conditions, avoid famous test items, compare to humans under like conditions, do not assume the same route as humans, check generalisation beyond one test, do not jump to conclusions.
numbers: 14 considerations listed (DO or DO NOT).
limits: A perspective, not data.
agent_relevance: A direct checklist for the agent's own self-evaluations; it mirrors animal-cognition practice (controls, triangulation, transfer).

source: Milliere & Rathkopf (2025) Anthropocentric bias in language model evaluation
finding: Names two opposite errors: auxiliary oversight (blaming competence when auxiliary factors caused the failure) and mechanistic chauvinism (calling a non-human strategy not real competence). This is the over-reading problem in both directions.
numbers: No new data; conceptual article in Computational Linguistics.
limits: Philosophical argument.
agent_relevance: Use both: a failed probe may be an auxiliary-factor failure (format, token budget), and a pass by an odd route is still a pass for that route. Treat limits as claims about a specific mechanism and task.
